text: 3.2 New Logistics Requirements Advanced energy technologies present risks and uncertainties related to weight, size, safety, and ease of assembly and disassembly. Advanced energy systems have varied sets of logistics demands, and the military adoption of these technologies will require updating protocols, including servicing, storage, transportation, and disposal (Lutton 2024). DOW could face higher costs and implementation delays while updating regulations and possibly safety or performance shortfalls if new technologies are adopted before logistics norms are fully adjusted. Expanding battery adoption requires planning for transportation, charging, lifetimes, safety, and end-of-life management. New, end-of-life, and damaged, defective, or recalled batteries require distinct handling procedures, with end-of-life and damaged batteries requiring more stringent handling due to their potential hazards, such as leaking harmful electrolyte or fire risks from thermal runaway events. Heavier batteries require extra measures to prevent thermal events during transportation (Khabur 2025). For military applications, batteries might need to remain in storage for extended periods and still be ready for immediate deployment when needed, and safety risks associated with such storage need to be considered. Moreover, DOW batteries are sometimes used in more extreme environments than commercial applications, reducing battery lifetimes and introducing uncertainty into safety protocols. Current battery technology remains relatively heavy compared to conventional diesel fuel, and EVs with lithium-ion (Li-ion) batteries tend to be 30% heavier than gas-powered vehicles, requiring adjustments in heavy-lift plans for deployment (Center for Transportation Research n.d.; NLR 2024b). 7 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. Li-ion batteries require different safety and fire-suppression protocols than petroleum fuels. While gasoline is a flammable liquid, Li-ion batteries, which are labeled as Class 9 hazardous materials by the U.S. Department of Transportation, pose other safety risks such as chemical leakage or even explosions under certain conditions (FAA 2016). Gasoline tank fires can be extinguished with foam-based systems, but Li-ion fires need significant amounts of water to prevent thermal runaway (U.S. Antarctic Program 2022). If thermal runaway occurs, extinguishing the resulting fire with common ABC fire extinguishers would be difficult and could release toxic gases (NLR 2023b; Thomas Edison Electric 2025). Li-ion batteries are generally safer when transported at a lower state of charge, and the International Civil Aviation Organization mandates that Li-ion batteries be transported at or below a 30% state of charge (PRBA 2015), suggesting that DOW will need to determine the acceptable risk of a potential flare-up event versus the risk of arriving in a combat zone with a lower state of charge. Hydrogen has a relatively high energy density by mass that could make it suitable for heavy-duty vehicles, ships, and aircraft, and such applications are being explored. Storing hydrogen requires much larger volumes than legacy fuels to achieve comparable energy output (Bhuiyan and Siddique 2025). Hydrogen is stored, compressed, and dispensed at high pressures, so infrastructure components such as compression, storage, and purification systems must be integrated (DOE HFTO 2025a).
